segments.t: In the executive office, the celebration is cut short as Hicham discovers that ASK just lost two huge stars. Infuriated by rival agency StarMédia, he demands an immediate counterattack: poaching iconic actor Fabrice Luchini. Let's listen to the tense confrontation in French first.
C'est quoi cette histoire avec Ramzy et Virginie Efira?
Ils ont rompu, et François Bréhier en a profité.
Bréhier dirige notre agence concurrente, StarMedia.
Ils nous ont volé nos acteurs!
Alors prenons leur plus grande star, Fabrice Luchini.
Vous ne pouvez pas nous demander de voler un client.
Pourquoi pas? Eux, ils l'ont fait.
Luchini est chez Bréhier depuis trente-cinq ans!
Il ne partira jamais de chez eux.
Je veux Luchini chez ASK avant la fin du mois.
Sinon, je peux vendre mes parts à StarMedia.
C'est une vengeance ridicule!
Un talent, il faut se battre pour lui.
Je vais chercher Luchini!
Let's examine how Hicham pushes his agents to take extreme risks.
C'est quoi cette histoire avec Ramzy et Virginie Efira?
'What is this story about Ramzy and Virginie Efira?' Hicham demands an explanation. This casual expression translates literally as 'it is what, this story'. The French use this structure often.
Ils ont rompu, et François Bréhier en a profité.

'They broke up, and François Bréhier took advantage of it.' Mathias explains the crisis. A common term meaning to take advantage is joined by a piece meaning 'of it'. In French, this phrasing is common.
Bréhier dirige notre agence concurrente, StarMedia.
'Bréhier runs our rival agency, StarMédia.' Mathias identifies the competitor. The term for a rival or competing group is built from a root meaning to compete. You will find this useful in French.
Ils nous ont volé nos acteurs!
'They stole our actors from us!' Hicham accuses the rival agency of theft. He uses a handy chunk meaning 'to us' right before the action of stealing. This sounds extremely natural in French.
Alors prenons leur plus grande star, Fabrice Luchini.
'So let us take their biggest star, Fabrice Luchini.' Hicham proposes a counterattack. A useful expression meaning biggest literally translates as 'more big'. In French, this is perfectly fine.
Vous ne pouvez pas nous demander de voler un client.

'You cannot ask us to steal a client.' Mathias raises a professional objection. He starts with a polite 'you' and a common expression meaning to be able to, in the negative. A standard way to speak in French.
Pourquoi pas? Eux, ils l'ont fait.
'Why not? They did it.' Hicham argues back. He uses an emphatic form for 'them' to contrast the rivals with his own team. In French, you will hear this.
Luchini est chez Bréhier depuis trente-cinq ans!
'Luchini has been with Bréhier for thirty-five years!' Andréa emphasizes the loyalty. A handy term translates as 'at the place of' to show where someone works or lives. The French say this often.
Il ne partira jamais de chez eux.
'He will never leave them.' Andréa asserts that poaching is impossible. The structure for 'never' wraps around the core action, much like standard negative phrases. In French, this is quite common.
Je veux Luchini chez ASK avant la fin du mois.
'I want Luchini at ASK before the end of the month.' Hicham sets a strict deadline. The term for the end is used here to set a boundary in time. This is how you say it in French.
Sinon, je peux vendre mes parts à StarMedia.
'Otherwise, I can sell my shares to StarMédia.' Hicham threatens his new team. The term for shares literally means parts or portions of a company. A handy phrase in French.
C'est une vengeance ridicule!
'It is a ridiculous revenge!' Mathias protests the irrational plan. The term for revenge is paired with a descriptor that looks exactly like its familiar cognate. A useful expression in French.
Un talent, il faut se battre pour lui.
'A talent, you have to fight for them.' Andréa expresses her instinct to compete. A common chunk meaning 'it is necessary' is used to show obligation. This is very typical in French.
Je vais chercher Luchini!

'I am going to get Luchini!' Andréa accepts the high-stakes mission. She uses a term meaning to search or look for, which here implies fetching someone. A common chunk in French. Now let's listen to the argument about Fabrice Luchini again at natural speed.

Ils nous ont volé nos acteurs!
Alors prenons leur plus grande star, Fabrice Luchini.

Il ne partira jamais de chez eux.

Sinon, je peux vendre mes parts à StarMedia.

Un talent, il faut se battre pour lui.
Je vais chercher Luchini!
Hicham has made his ultimatum clear: sign Fabrice Luchini or risk losing the entire agency. While Mathias panics, Andréa prepares to make contact with the great actor. See you next time!
Au revoir!
